titre: The age of the Earth fit in a trace of lead
accroche: In 1956, a geochemist measures the age of the Earth at 4.55 billion years. In trying to refine it, he discovers something else entirely.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1956, the American geochemist Clair Patterson published an eight-page paper in *Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta*, titled “Age of meteorites and the earth.” The figure he calculates there, 4.55 billion years, give or take 70 million, remains the reference for the age of the Earth today.

## A lead clock

Patterson's method rests on the radioactive decay of uranium into lead, at a known and constant rate. Measuring the proportions of lead isotopes in a rock should therefore, in theory, make it possible to date its formation. The problem, on Earth, is that rocks have been recycled and reworked so many times by tectonics that they no longer record the age of the planet itself. Patterson gets around the obstacle by analyzing meteorites, in particular the Canyon Diablo meteorite, from Arizona, formed, like the Earth, from the same original dust cloud but geologically inert ever since. Their age is that of the solar system, and therefore, more or less, that of the Earth.

## An unexpected obstacle

To measure such minute traces of lead, Patterson must first make sure nothing contaminates his samples. He then discovers that lead is everywhere, in the air, in laboratory dust, even in his own reagents, at concentrations that make any reliable measurement impossible without a level of clean-room work unprecedented for the time. This hunt for contamination leads him to a discovery that goes far beyond the dating of meteorites: the lead in the ambient environment is not natural.

## The real impact

In 1962, with Tsaihwa J. Chow, Patterson shows that ocean sediments receive about eighty times more lead than natural erosion of rocks would explain. Greenland ice cores confirm a hundredfold increase in the lead load during the 20th century. The source: leaded gasoline, widespread since the 1920s to reduce engine knock. Patterson then spends two decades documenting and publicly denouncing this contamination, against an industry that funds contradictory studies and tries to have him removed from federal scientific committees.

## What this shifts

The fight succeeds: the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, created on December 2, 1970, receives most of its powers by the end of that same month, with the amended Clean Air Act, and gradually reduces and then bans lead in road gasoline, up to the total ban on January 1, 1996. Patterson's most-cited result is therefore not the one we remember first, the date of the Earth's birth, but the one he brought to light while trying to refine it with enough rigor to notice that the ambient air should not have contained what it did.

repere.texte: In 1956, Clair Patterson calculates the age of the Earth at 4.55 billion years (± 70 million), from the lead in the Canyon Diablo meteorite, a figure still used today. While hunting down contamination in his samples, he discovers that ocean sediments receive about 80 times more lead than natural erosion would explain, and that the lead load in the atmosphere increased 100-fold during the 20th century.
repere.source: National Academy of Sciences, biographical memoir of Clair C. Patterson

carte.punch: He measured the age of the Earth, and discovered that the air shouldn't contain this.
carte.idee: In 1956, Clair Patterson calculates the age of the Earth at 4.55 billion years using the lead in a meteorite. In trying to purify his measurements, he discovers widespread contamination from leaded gasoline, and spends two decades fighting it, until it is banned in the United States.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: A fuller portrait of the man and of his clean-room measurement method.

quiz.question: Why did Clair Patterson use a meteorite rather than an Earth rock to date the Earth?
choix: Because Earth rocks have been recycled too much by tectonics to retain a record of the planet's age
Because no Earth rock contains a measurable amount of lead
Because meteorites are easier to date than rocks, whatever their origin
Because lead dating only works on extraterrestrial rocks
quiz.explication: Earth rocks have been melted, recycled, and reworked by plate tectonics: they therefore no longer record the age of the planet itself. Meteorites like Canyon Diablo formed at the same time as the Earth, from the same original cloud, but have remained geologically inert ever since.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why was gasoline leaded starting in the 1920s?
choix: To lower the cost of refining fuel
To extend the shelf life of the fuel
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Leaded gasoline became widespread starting in the 1920s to reduce engine knock. Patterson identified it as the source of the lead he kept finding everywhere, even in his own reagents.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the measurements published by Patterson and Chow in 1962 show?
choix: That the lead in the oceans came mostly from underwater volcanoes
That ocean sediments receive nearly 80 times too much lead
That Earth rocks had lost their lead through erosion
That laboratory air was cleaner than city air
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Ocean sediments were receiving about eighty times more lead than natural erosion of rocks would explain. Greenland ice cores confirmed a hundredfold increase in the lead load during the 20th century.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did industry respond to Patterson's work on lead?
choix: By funding contradictory studies and trying to have him removed
By voluntarily removing lead from gasoline as early as the 1960s
By adopting his measurements as its own and making them public
By refraining from reacting, having no arguments to counter the measurements
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Patterson spent two decades documenting and publicly denouncing this contamination, facing an industry that funded contradictory studies and tried to have him removed from federal scientific committees.
